entries.meaning: Ravana asks who Hanuman is, by whose power he ruined the grove, whether he has not heard of Ravana, why he killed demons, and why he does not fear death. Hanuman names the power that fashions the cosmos through maya, by which Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva create, sustain, and dissolve; Shesha bears the worlds, the divine Protector assumes bodies, Shiva's bow was broken, kings humbled, and Khara, Dushana, Trishira, and Bali slain. Ravana's own victories derive from a trace of that power. Hanuman declares himself messenger of the Lord whose beloved wife Ravana abducted.

Hanuman says he knows Ravana's prowess from his encounters with Sahasrabahu and Bali. He ate fruit from hunger and broke trees by monkey nature; the guards attacked him, so he defended the body dear to all. Ravana's son bound him only because Hanuman wished to accomplish Rama's task. With folded hands he counsels Ravana to consider his lineage, abandon delusion, worship the remover of devotees' fear, avoid enmity with the Lord feared even by Time, and return Janaki. Compassionate Rama protects those who surrender and forgets their offences.

Hanuman urges Ravana to hold Rama's lotus feet in his heart and rule Lanka securely, not stain the spotless moonlike fame of sage Pulastya's line. Speech without Rama's name is unbecoming, like a richly ornamented woman without clothing. Wealth and power turned from Rama vanish even when gained, like rain-fed streams without perennial springs. Hanuman vows that no one protects one hostile to Rama—not even a thousand Shivas, Vishnus, or Brahmas—and tells Ravana to abandon pride rooted in delusion and productive of pain, and worship Rama, ocean of grace.

Though Hanuman's highly beneficial speech is steeped in devotion, discernment, dispassion, and policy, proud Ravana laughs that he has found a learned monkey-teacher and threatens death. Hanuman replies that Ravana's reversal is evident. Furious, Ravana orders him killed, but Vibhishana arrives with ministers and invokes diplomatic law: an envoy must not be killed; another punishment should be used. Ravana orders the monkey mutilated and sent away—above all, burn the tail monkeys cherish, wrapping it in oil-soaked cloth.

Ravana expects the tailless monkey to return with his master so Ravana can see their power. Hanuman smiles, recognizing Sarasvati's help in Ravana's order. The demons wrap his tail, but Hanuman lengthens it playfully until Lanka runs out of cloth, ghee, and oil. Citizens kick and mock him, parade him with drums and clapping, then light the tail. Hanuman instantly becomes tiny, slips free, climbs a golden roof, and terrifies the demon women. At Hari's prompting the forty-nine winds blow; Hanuman expands skyward, laughing and roaring.

With an immense yet extremely light body, Hanuman races from mansion to mansion while Lanka burns. Terrified people cry for parents and rescuers, realizing that this is no ordinary monkey but a god in monkey-form, and that contempt for a saint bears such fruit. In an instant the city burns except Vibhishana's house. Shiva explains that fire, created by Hanuman's own Lord, could not burn his messenger. Hanuman thoroughly burns Lanka, leaps into the ocean, extinguishes his tail, relieves fatigue, resumes a small form, and stands before Janaka's daughter with folded hands.

Hanuman asks Sita for a token like the one Rama gave him. She removes her crest-jewel, and he receives it joyfully. Her message bows to the all-fulfilled Lord and asks him to remember his renown as compassionate to the lowly and remove her great distress. Hanuman must recount the episode of Indra's son and remind Rama of his arrow's power. If Rama does not arrive within a month, he will not find her alive. Sita asks how to preserve life when Hanuman too leaves: seeing him cooled her heart, but now the same days and nights return. After consoling her repeatedly, Hanuman bows at her lotus feet and departs for Rama.

Departing, Hanuman roars so thunderously that demon women miscarry. He crosses the ocean and gives the waiting monkeys a jubilant cry. Seeing him, they rejoice as if newly born; his bright face and radiant body show that Rama's task is done. They meet him like thirsting fish finding water and set off joyfully toward Rama, exchanging the new story. In Madhuvana, with Angada's consent, they eat fruit and drive away protesting guards with fists. When the guards report the prince has wrecked the grove, Sugriva rejoices: the monkeys must have accomplished the Lord's task.

Sugriva reasons that without finding Sita the monkeys would not dare eat Madhuvana's fruit. They arrive as a company, bow to him, and are embraced lovingly. Seeing them at his feet, Sugriva asks their welfare; through Rama's grace the exceptional task is accomplished. He praises Hanuman for saving every monkey's life, embraces him, and leads the company to Rama. Rama rejoices on seeing they have succeeded. The brothers sit on a crystal slab as all the monkeys fall at their feet; compassionate Rama embraces them and asks their welfare. They answer that beholding his lotus feet is welfare itself.

Jambavan tells Rama that whoever receives his mercy is always blessed and safe, with gods, humans, and sages pleased; that person becomes victorious, humble, virtuous, and renowned through the three worlds. Rama's grace completed everything and made their birth fruitful. Hanuman's deed cannot be described by a thousand mouths. After hearing the account, delighted Rama embraces Hanuman and asks how Janaki lives and protects her life. Hanuman answers: Rama's name is her day-and-night guard, meditation on him her door, and her eyes are locked upon her own feet—by what path could life depart?
